implementation_notes: Kotlin makes classes and their members final by default (data, enum and sealed classes are closed by design), so a test-only subclass can only override a member that production deliberately marked open - which inverts the pattern's 'no production change' premise into 'edit production to open the seam'. Where the code is yours, extract the boundary behind an interface and inject a fake; where it is not, MockK's instrumentation mocks final classes and members without inheritance (spyk, mockkClass), which is a different mechanism from a test-specific subclass. Because override is mandatory in Kotlin, a member that fails to override is a compile error rather than a silently real call.
pitfalls: A missing open on the class or the member is a hard compile error for the test - safer than a silent real call, but it forces an edit to production code.
MockK's mockkStatic/mockkConstructor/mockkObject transform classes globally for the process and must be undone (unmockk*, clearAllMocks) or later tests observe the mocks.

internal members are visible to the test source set only because of the build tool's module concept, not because there is an inheritance seam - moving tests to another Gradle module removes the access.
alternative: Extract the boundary behind an interface and inject a fake (Dependency Injection), or mock final members with MockK's instrumentation (spyk/mockkClass) - Kotlin's final-by-default classes turn the inheritance seam into a production edit.
